turns.prompt_text: In I believe it's one of the second or later movies of The Chronicles of Narnia. They revive the ice witch
turns.response_html:
You are exactly right. That happens in the second film of the trilogy, The Chronicles of Narnia: Prince Caspian (2008).

The Resurrection Scene

The scene takes place inside Aslan's How after the Narnians suffer a devastating, failed night raid on King Miraz's castle. Desperate and grieving the loss of his soldiers, Prince Caspian is approached by the cynical black dwarf, Nikabrik.

Nikabrik claims he knows a power that can defeat the Telmarines when Aslan cannot be found. He introduces Caspian to two sinister figures: a Hag and a Werewolf.

How the Ritual Works

  • The Magic: The Hag uses dark sorcery and blood magic to conjure an enormous, towering wall of blue ice.
  • The Apparition: The spirit of Jadis, the White Witch (played by Tilda Swinton), materializes inside the frozen pane.
  • The Price: Because she was killed by Aslan in the first movie (The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe), she cannot return on her own. She extends her hand through the frost, tempting Caspian, and then Peter Pevensie, telling them that just a single drop of "Adam's blood" will completely release her back into the living world.

The Resolution

Just as Peter is entranced and stepping forward to touch her hand, Edmund Pevensie rushes into the chamber. Remembering the horror of her rule firsthand from the first film, Edmund drives his sword straight into the back of the ice wall.

The pane shatters into thousands of harmless shards, completely destroying the spell and stopping her resurrection just seconds before she can break free.

turns.prompt_text: Why were they going to figure in the first place? And my recollection, I thought they did for her, but I can't recall.
turns.response_html:
That part of the story boils down to sheer desperation, and you are completely right to remember her coming back later—your memory isn't playing tricks on you, it's just jumping ahead to the next movie!

Here is exactly why they turned to her in Prince Caspian, and where she actually makes her big return.

Why They Turned to Her: Ruthless Pragmatism

The Narnian rebellion was completely falling apart. They had just launched a massive, unauthorized night raid on King Miraz’s castle, and it was an absolute slaughter. They lost a huge chunk of their army, morale was below zero, and Prince Caspian was drowning in guilt.

The dwarf Nikabrik represents a dark, cynical mindset. He is tired of waiting around for Aslan to show up and save them, and he doesn't think a bunch of human kids (the Pevensies) have what it takes to win a brutal, bloody war. His logic is simple, desperate, and ruthless: use a monster to destroy a monster.

"I'll believe in anyone or anything that'll batter these cursed Telmarine barbarians to pieces... Anyone or anything, Aslan or the White Witch, do you understand?"

To Nikabrik, the White Witch was a practical weapon. She had held Narnia in an iron grip for a century, and he knew she possessed the raw, terrifying magic necessary to pulverize the Telmarines. He didn't care about the consequences of letting her loose; he just wanted to win the war happening right in front of him.

Why You Remember Her Coming Back: The Voyage of the Dawn Treader

You are likely remembering the third film, where Tilda Swinton does return to haunt the characters, which is probably why you recall them dealing with her again.

In The Voyage of the Dawn Treader (2010), the crew encounters a sentient, evil Green Mist that materializes from the Dark Island. This mist feeds on a person's deepest, darkest psychological insecurities and turns them into illusions.

Because Edmund still carries massive trauma from the first movie and secretly envies his older brother Peter, the Mist manifests as the White Witch. She appears to him as a glowing, ghostly phantom, whispering in his ear, offering him ultimate power, and tempting him to become her king.

So while Edmund successfully shatters her physical resurrection in Prince Caspian, she absolutely returns as a terrifying mental phantom in the very next movie to try and corrupt him all over again.

turns.prompt_text: I read The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe when I was little and I watched the movies. But I haven't for a while and I haven't read the books in a while. I don't think I ever completely read all the books.
turns.response_html:
That is incredibly common. The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe gets almost all the spotlight, and the movies from the 2000s are a massive wave of nostalgia for a lot of people.

The full series actually spans seven books, but Hollywood only adapted the first three before the film franchise lost steam. If you only watched the movies, you missed out on some of C.S. Lewis's weirdest and coolest world-building.

The Narnia Books You Might Have Missed

If you ever decide to dive back into them, the books that never made it to the big screen completely shift focus away from the standard Pevensie timeline:

  • The Magician's Nephew: A prequel that explains the literal creation of Narnia. It reveals where the White Witch actually came from (a dying world called Charn), why a random lamppost is growing in the middle of a snowy woods, and how the magic wardrobe was built.
  • The Silver Chair: This takes place right after The Voyage of the Dawn Treader. Eustace (the cousin) returns to Narnia with a classmate named Jill. They are sent to find an elderly King Caspian’s missing son, who has been trapped underground by a new witch.
  • The Horse and His Boy: A total detour. It takes place during the reign of the Pevensie siblings when they are adults ruling from Cair Paravel. It focuses on a young boy escaping a southern empire alongside a talking Narnian horse.
  • The Last Battle: The final book. It is a pretty intense, apocalyptic conclusion where Narnia faces its end, and Lewis leans heavily into his grander mythological and theological themes.

Because of how the books are structured, readers usually split into two camps: those who read them in the order they were published, and those who read them chronologically (starting with the prequel).

Would you be more interested in hearing about how the whole world of Narnia actually started in the prequel, or what happens to the characters after the movie timeline ends?

turns.prompt_text: A little bit. Why did the author write these this way? Was it about World War II?
turns.response_html:
World War II didn't just influence the books—it is the exact reason the story exists.

The World War II Connection

While the books are not a direct political allegory, the war provided the literal framework and atmosphere for the entire narrative.

  • The Real Evacuees: In 1939, during the threat of the London Blitz, the British government shipped millions of children out to rural areas for safety. C.S. Lewis opened his own country home, The Kilns, to a group of evacuated schoolgirls. Observing these children staying in his house—and noticing how few imaginative stories they knew—directly inspired the concept of the Pevensie children being sent to the Professor's house. In fact, one of the real-world evacuees was fascinated by an old wardrobe on the property.
  • Wartime Rationing: Edmund’s infamous betrayal of his siblings for a box of Turkish Delight carries a lot more weight in a wartime context. In 1940s Britain, sugar, chocolate, and sweets were strictly rationed and incredibly rare. To a child of that era, the promise of unlimited candy was a massive, genuinely overwhelming temptation.
  • The Atmosphere of Occupation: The White Witch’s tyrannical grip on Narnia—ensuring it is "always winter but never Christmas"—strongly mirrored the bleak, frozen, and hopeless feeling of living in Nazi-occupied Europe during the dark days of the war.

Why the Books Were Written "This Way"

The reason the series feels beautifully chaotic, leaping from direct sequels to ancient prequels (The Magician's Nephew) and strange side-quests (The Horse and His Boy), is that Lewis never had a grand master plan.

He did not sit down to sketch out a massive, interconnected seven-book epic. Instead, he started with a single visual image that had been stuck in his mind since he was 16 years old: a Faun carrying an umbrella and parcels through a snowy wood. He wrote The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe around that image just to see where it went.

When the book became a massive success, he decided to keep expanding the boundaries of the world. Because Lewis was an Oxford professor of medieval and renaissance literature, his mind was a treasure trove of ancient folklore. He structured subsequent books around the themes and mythologies he loved most, seamlessly blending:

  • Greek and Roman Myths: Centaurs, nymphs, and the wine god Bacchus.
  • Norse Mythology: Giants, deep winters, and the literal apocalyptic ending of the world in The Last Battle.
  • Theology: Strong moral philosophy, questions of faith, and redemption.

Ultimately, he chose this fairy-tale format because he believed a grand, imaginative myth was the best way to help a generation of war-weary children process heavy themes like loss, loyalty, sacrifice, and the triumph of good over evil.

For a deeper look into how personal military service and the psychological toll of the Blitz influenced the creators of both Narnia and Middle-earth, How the World Wars Shaped J.R.R. Tolkien and C.S. Lewis provides incredible historical context on how these authors processed modern warfare through the lens of fantasy.
